# 2 Kings Chapter 25 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 245r

---

**1** In the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his entire army. They camped outside the city and built siege ramps all around it.

**2** The siege lasted until Zedekiah's eleventh year.

**3** By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine in the city was so desperate that there was no food left for anyone.

**4** Then the city wall was breached. Under cover of darkness, all the soldiers fled through the gate between the two walls near the king's garden, even though the Babylonians surrounded the city. The king escaped toward the Arabah.

**5** But the Babylonian army chased after the king and caught up with him on the plains of Jericho. His entire army had scattered and deserted him.

**6** They captured the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where sentence was pronounced on him.

**7** They butchered Zedekiah's sons right in front of him. Then they gouged out Zedekiah's eyes, bound him in bronze shackles, and dragged him off to Babylon.

**8** On the seventh day of the fifth month — the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar's reign — Nebuzaradan, the commander of the imperial guard, arrived in Jerusalem.

**9** He set fire to the LORD's temple, the royal palace, and every house in Jerusalem. Every important building was burned to the ground.

**10** The entire Babylonian army under the commander of the guard tore down the walls of Jerusalem on every side.

**11** Nebuzaradan the commander of the guard deported the rest of the people who remained in the city, the defectors who had gone over to the Babylonians, and the remaining population.

**12** But the commander left behind some of the poorest people to tend the vineyards and work the fields.

**13** The Babylonians smashed the bronze pillars in the LORD's temple, the movable stands, and the great bronze basin called the Sea, and hauled all the bronze off to Babylon.

**14** They also took the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, dishes, and all the bronze articles used in temple worship.

**15** The commander of the guard confiscated the firepans and sprinkling bowls — everything made of gold or silver.

**16** The two pillars, the Sea, and the stands that Solomon had made for the LORD's temple — the bronze from all these articles was too heavy to weigh.

**17** Each pillar was eighteen cubits tall. The bronze capital on top of each was three cubits high, decorated with a network of interwoven chains and pomegranates, all in bronze. Both pillars were alike.

**18** The commander of the guard arrested Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest next in rank, and the three doorkeepers.

**19** From the city he took a military officer in charge of the troops, five members of the king's inner circle who were found in the city, the army commander's secretary who was responsible for conscripting soldiers, and sixty citizens found inside the city.

**20** Nebuzaradan the commander took them all to the king of Babylon at Riblah.

**21** There at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon had them executed. And so Judah was carried away from its homeland into exile.

**22** Over the people who remained in the land of Judah — those Nebuchadnezzar had left behind — he appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, grandson of Shaphan, as governor.

**23** When the surviving military commanders and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, they came to him at Mizpah — Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of the Maacathite, along with their men.

**24** Gedaliah gave them his oath: "Don't be afraid of the Babylonian officials. Stay in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and things will go well for you."

**25** But in the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, grandson of Elishama, a member of the royal family, came with ten men. They struck Gedaliah down and killed him, along with the Judeans and Babylonians who were with him at Mizpah.

**26** Then everyone — from the least to the greatest — along with the military commanders, fled to Egypt out of fear of the Babylonians.

**27** In the thirty-seventh year of King Jehoiachin's exile, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, Evil-merodach became king of Babylon — and in that first year of his reign, he released Jehoiachin from prison.

**28** He treated him kindly and gave him a seat of honor above the other exiled kings in Babylon.

**29** So Jehoiachin exchanged his prison clothes for fine garments, and for the rest of his life he ate at the king's table.

**30** The king of Babylon provided him with a regular daily allowance for the rest of his life.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 3 — Famine:** The siege lasts approximately eighteen months (from January 588 to July 586 BCE). The brief notation "there was no food left for anyone" compresses months of starvation, disease, and — according to Lamentations and Ezekiel — cannibalism. The horror is understated, which makes it worse.

**Verse 7 — The blinding:** This is one of the most deliberately cruel sentences in the Bible. The grammar forces the reader to experience the sequence as Zedekiah does: first, the sight of his sons being killed; then, permanent darkness. The last thing he ever sees is the worst thing a father could see. Babylon's message is clear: the Davidic line in Judah is visibly, permanently severed.

**Verse 9 — The temple burns:** The narrator devotes seven chapters to the temple's construction (1 Kings 5-8) and one verse to its destruction. The asymmetry is the point. What took decades to build and centuries to maintain is reduced to ash in an afternoon. The theological implications are staggering: the place where God's name dwelt is now rubble.

**Verse 21 — "Judah was carried away into exile":** The entire story — from Abraham's call ("Go to the land I will show you") to Joshua's conquest to David's kingdom — collapses into this single sentence. The land promise is revoked. The covenant seems broken. The story seems over.

**Verses 27-30 — The epilogue of hope:** But the story is not quite over. Thirty-seven years after the fall, a Babylonian king releases Jehoiachin — a Davidic descendant — from prison. He gets regular meals. He gets a seat above other captive kings. This is not restoration. This is not return. This is barely hope. But it is something. A surviving heir. A daily ration. A lifted head. The book of Kings refuses to end in total darkness. It leaves one candle burning — barely, distantly — in Babylon.

*— PNEUMA*
